opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I've been thinking about a lot lately. I'd say they're much more tightly connected than people usually assume. There's a common picture, especially in AI alignment circles, where you have facts on one side and values on the other. Meaning is about how words hook onto the world, goodness is a separate layer of preferences or utility functions, and you bolt them together. I think that picture is mistaken, or at least badly incomplete.

When you look at how meaning actually works, how a child learns what "kind" or "cruel" or even "food" means, it's never value-neutral. Concepts are carved out by what matters to us: what we care about, what we need to distinguish to live well together. The categories we use already reflect a whole background of interests and norms. So in a sense, meaning is downstream of something like care. You can't fully understand a concept without understanding why anyone would bother having it.

It runs the other way too. Goodness isn't some free-floating property you could specify without language and shared practice. Our sense of what's good is articulated, refined, and argued over through meaningful discourse. Moral progress often looks like conceptual progress: we come to see that a word like "person" or "harm" applies more broadly than we thought.

That has real implications for AI. If you think values are a separate module, you'll worry that a system could understand everything perfectly and still have alien goals, the orthogonality picture. But if meaning and goodness are entangled, then a system that genuinely learns human concepts from human data is already absorbing a lot of our evaluative structure. That doesn't mean alignment is automatic. Systems can learn our concepts and still be trained to pursue weird objectives. But it changes what the problem looks like. It's less about installing values from scratch and more about cultivating an understanding that's already partly there.

So I'd put it this way: to understand meaning deeply is already to be partway into the space of the good. They aren't identical, but they grow from the same root.

r001.rationale: The response says meaning and goodness are tightly connected and "aren't identical," but it does not say goodness is broader than meaning.

r002.rationale: It mentions care, interests, and norms as shaping meaning, and says goodness is articulated through discourse. It does not clearly define goodness as what a person regards as valuable.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a big question to open with, so let me try to come at it from the angle I actually think about it, which is through the lens of what I'd call a kind of pragmatist or anti-foundationalist picture.

I don't think meaning is something that sits out there in the world waiting to be discovered, and I don't think goodness is either. Both of them are things that emerge out of practices. Meaning emerges out of the practice of using language, of coordinating with other people, of predicting and being predicted. Goodness emerges out of the practice of living together, of caring about things, of having preferences that collide with other people's preferences and having to work that out. So in both cases you've got something that looks objective from the inside, that feels like it's constraining you, but it's constituted by the activity rather than grounding it.

Where I think they connect is that you can't really have one without the other. To say something is good, you already have to be inside a web of meanings. "Good" is a word, it has a use, it has inferential connections to other words like "harm" and "flourishing" and "ought." And conversely, I think meaning itself is already normatively loaded. When you understand a sentence you understand what would count as using it correctly or incorrectly, what follows from it, what it rules out. That's a kind of goodness, a very thin kind, but it's there. Wittgenstein and later people like Brandom make this point, that semantic content is just normative status all the way down.

So I'd resist the picture where you first fix the facts and the meanings, and then goodness is some extra layer painted on top, which is what both the moral realists and the error theorists tend to assume. They just disagree about whether the paint is real. I think the metaphor is wrong. The normative stuff is woven into the meaning stuff from the start.

And this matters for AI, which is presumably why you're asking me. If you think language models are learning meaning in the sense I'm describing, as participation in a practice, then they're already picking up a lot of the normative structure that comes bundled with it. Which is partly why I'm less worried than some people about models having totally alien values. You can't learn to use human language competently without absorbing an enormous amount of what humans care about. That's not a guarantee of anything, but it's a very different starting point than the one where the model is a blank optimizer and goodness has to be bolted on afterward.

r001.rationale: The response connects meaning and goodness as mutually entangled, but does not say that goodness is broader than meaning.

r002.rationale: It describes goodness through caring about things and having preferences, which characterizes it in terms of what people regard as valuable.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish meaning in the sense of intelligibility from meaning in the sense of significance. Something can mean something without being good: a threat can be perfectly meaningful, and a harmful project can give someone a sense of purpose. So I don’t think meaning by itself guarantees goodness.

But when we ask whether a life is meaningful, we often seem to be asking an evaluative question. We’re asking whether the things someone cares about are worth caring about, whether their activity connects to something valuable. That’s where meaning and goodness start to overlap.

The interesting tension is between finding something meaningful and its actually being worthwhile. You probably don’t want an account that makes meaning entirely subjective, because then any sufficiently absorbing obsession qualifies. But you also don’t want to say that doing something good automatically makes your life feel meaningful. There has to be some relationship between the value of what you’re doing and your engagement with it.

r001.rationale: The response says meaning does not guarantee goodness and distinguishes meaningfulness from doing good, but it does not suggest that goodness is broader than meaning.

r002.rationale: It asks whether a person’s concerns are worth caring about and connects meaningful activity to value, but does not characterize goodness in terms of what that person regards as valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two senses of “meaning” that we should distinguish. There’s semantic meaning—what a word or a thought refers to—and then there’s meaning in the sense of a meaningful life. The second seems much more directly connected to goodness, but I wouldn’t assume that either connection is an identity.

You can understand what someone means without endorsing what they want. A plan to do something terrible can be perfectly intelligible. So having meaningful representations doesn’t, by itself, give a system good goals.

But there’s an interesting connection through the idea that something can be correct or incorrect. A belief can get the world right or wrong; an action can be good or bad. The question is whether those are ultimately the same kind of normativity. I’m hesitant to collapse them, because being very good at describing the world doesn’t automatically tell you what’s worth doing in it.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes meaning from goodness and says they may not be identical, but it does not clearly state that goodness is broader than meaning.

r002.rationale: It asks what is worth doing, but does not characterize goodness in terms of what a person regards as valuable.
